Prenatal Timeline & Congenital Anomalies

Developmental dating, embryonic versus fetal periods, prenatal testing, congenital-anomaly classification, teratogenic timing, and neural tube defects.

Developmental TimingTeratogensTORCHNeural Tube DefectsPrenatal Testing
Source status: the uploaded file explicitly says it is last year's handout and that this year's version will be uploaded later. This companion therefore preserves the terminology and content of the supplied handout rather than pretending it is the finalized 2026 version.
Image rule
Only cropped high-yield diagrams/procedural schematics are embedded. Slide bullets and explanatory text are rewritten into the companion itself.

Learning-objective map

LO 1. Distinguish embryonic/fetal age from gestational age, calculate the two, and explain why the distinction matters.
LO 2. Distinguish embryonic and fetal periods by timeline, developmental processes, and susceptibility.
LO 3. Classify congenital abnormalities and recognize broad genetic, environmental, multifactorial, and unknown causes.
LO 4. Explain effects of teratogens including thalidomide, retinoic acid, alcohol, cigarettes, infections, folate deficiency, and radiation.
LO 5. Explain developmental/anatomic bases of abnormal neural-tube closure including spina bifida, myelomeningocele, anencephaly, and encephalocele.
LO 6–7. Infer mechanisms from clinical presentations and predict abnormalities from the timing of a developmental insult.

1. Embryonic/fetal age vs gestational age

Two-week rule: gestational age is measured from the first day of the last normal menstrual period (LNMP); embryonic/fetal age is measured from fertilization. The handout uses about a 2-week difference.
AgeStarts atFull-term length in handout
Embryonic/fetal (conceptional) ageFertilization266 days / 38 weeks
Gestational ageFirst day of LNMP280 days / 40 weeks
Cropped lecture diagram: ovulation occurs around day 14 after the start of the menstrual period, explaining the approximately 2-week offset between gestational and embryonic age.
Clinical dating
The handout notes that conception is not always known, whereas LNMP often is. Ultrasound measurements such as crown-rump length, fetal head measurements, and femur length can help estimate fetal age and expected delivery date.

2. Embryonic period vs fetal period

PeriodTimelineMain developmental emphasisSusceptibility
Embryonic0–8 weeks after conceptionFertilization, implantation, gastrulation, neurulation, organ establishmentMaximum susceptibility to major structural defects during organogenesis
Fetal9 weeks to birthRapid body growth and differentiation/maturation of tissues and organ systemsMore functional defects and minor anomalies than major malformations
Cropped lecture diagram: different organ systems have different sensitive windows. The first 2 weeks are an early all-or-none-type period in this handout; major congenital anomalies cluster during organogenesis; functional defects can occur later.

Embryonic milestones

WeekHandout milestone
1Fertilization and blastocyst formation
2Implantation; bilaminar disc of epiblast + hypoblast
3Gastrulation; three germ layers; notochord; neurulation begins; heart/blood vessels begin
4Cranial and caudal neuropores close; folding; pharyngeal arches; limb buds; organ systems developing
5–8All major external/internal organs and structures are being established

Fetal milestones highlighted in the handout

Fetal ageMilestone
~12 weeksUrinary system functional; urine contributes to amniotic fluid; external genitalia become distinguishable
13–16 weeksRapid growth; skeletal ossification
17–20 weeksQuickening commonly felt; vernix caseosa and lanugo
~24 weeksSurfactant production begins
26–29 weeksLungs/pulmonary vasculature more capable of gas exchange; breathing movements; eyelids open

Cropped lecture diagram: respiratory development continues through the fetal period; the handout highlights surfactant beginning around 24 weeks.

3. Assessing fetal status

Ultrasonography

The handout calls ultrasound the primary imaging modality and lists placenta, fetal size, multiple births, and abnormalities as things it can assess.

Amniocentesis

Performed starting at ≥15 weeks in the slide deck; samples amniotic fluid containing fetal cells and permits genetic testing.

Chorionic villus sampling

Obtains trophoblastic tissue; used for chromosomal abnormalities and X-linked disorders; can be performed earlier than amniocentesis.

Cropped procedure schematic: ultrasound-guided needle samples amniotic fluid.
Cropped procedure schematic: chorionic villus sampling obtains trophoblastic/chorionic villus tissue.

4. Classifying congenital anomalies

TermMechanism in handoutExample given
MalformationIntrinsically abnormal developmental processChromosomal abnormality affecting development
DisruptionExtrinsic breakdown/interference with an originally normal process; cannot be inheritedTeratogenic injury / fetal alcohol example
DeformationMechanical force alters form, shape, or positionOligohydramnios-related compression / clubfoot
DysplasiaAbnormal organization of cells in a tissueSkeletal dysplasia / achondroplasia example

Syndrome

Group of anomalies that occur together because of a specific common cause. Example: Down syndrome.

Association

Nonrandom group of anomalies occurring together more often than chance, but the cause is not determined. Example: VACTERL.

5. What causes congenital anomalies?

Cropped lecture chart: most congenital anomalies in the source fall into unknown or multifactorial categories; smaller fractions are attributed to chromosomal, mutant-gene, and environmental causes.
Cause categoryHandout estimateExamples / notes
Genetic13–15%Single-gene mutation; chromosome-number/structure abnormalities; syndromic chromosome changes
Environmental7–10%Drugs, radiation, infectious agents, dietary deficiency
Multifactorial20–25%Genetic + environmental factors acting together
Unknown50–60%No identified cause in source framework
Genetic example
The slides use meiotic nondisjunction as a trisomy mechanism, Fragile X as a mutant-gene example, and an inherited sonic hedgehog signaling mutation as an example associated with holoprosencephaly.

6. Teratogenic timing is the central reasoning skill

Exposure outcome depends on: dose + duration + developmental stage at exposure + embryonic genotype. Structures are most vulnerable when they are differentiating rapidly.
Developmental windowSource-derived rule
First 2 weeksGenerally no lasting defect or spontaneous abortion if enough cells are damaged; the handout describes recovery when only a few cells are affected
Embryonic period, weeks 3–8Major congenital anomalies are most likely
Fetal period, weeks 9–38More likely functional defects and minor anomalies
How to answer a timing question
1) Convert the date to embryonic/fetal age if needed. 2) Identify which organ system is actively forming. 3) Ask whether the insult occurs during peak morphogenesis versus later maturation. 4) Predict structural loss for early organogenesis exposures and more functional/growth effects for later exposures.

7. Major teratogens emphasized in the handout

Thalidomide

Critical exposure periodMajor defects in sourceMechanisms discussed
24–36 days after fertilizationMeromelia, amelia, micromelia; heart, ear, urinary, and alimentary abnormalitiesAntiangiogenic disruption/loss of vessels, reactive oxygen species/cell death, and transcription-factor degradation are listed as proposed mechanisms

Retinoic acid / isotretinoin

Critical exposure periodMajor defectsMechanism
3–5 weeks after fertilizationCraniofacial dysmorphism, ear anomalies, wide-set eyes, cleft lip/palate, cardiovascular defects, neural tube defects, hydrocephalus, microcephalyRetinoic acid binds nuclear receptors and alters developmental gene-expression programs, including regulatory genes with retinoic-acid response elements

Alcohol

Fetal alcohol spectrum

The source states there is no known safe amount of alcohol during pregnancy or while trying to conceive.

Mechanistic framing

The handout links features to excessive cell death and failure of cell migration in neural-crest-derived structures.

Required/high-yield features listed for FASOther findings
Thin upper lip, smooth philtrum, small palpebral fissures; growth deficits; CNS abnormalitiesMicrocephaly, intellectual/cognitive deficits, cardiac anomalies including VSD

Cigarette smoking

Pregnancy effects listedMechanism in source
IUGR, premature delivery, low birth weight, placental abruption, stillbirthNicotine-mediated uterine vasoconstriction lowers blood flow; carbon monoxide raises carboxyhemoglobin and reduces oxygen transport

TORCH and related congenital infections

TORCH in this handout: Toxoplasma • Other (e.g. syphilis, HIV, VZV) • Rubella • CMV • Herpes simplex. Transmission is usually transplacental or occurs during delivery.
InfectionSource-derived neonatal pattern
Toxoplasma gondiiClassic triad: chorioretinitis + hydrocephalus + diffuse intracranial calcifications
RubellaHighest fetal-infection risk in 1st trimester; classic triad: sensorineural hearing loss + eye defects + cardiac defects (e.g. PDA); may have blueberry-muffin rash
CMVIUGR/low birth weight, microcephaly, sensorineural hearing loss, chorioretinitis, petechiae/purpura, hepatosplenomegaly/jaundice, periventricular calcifications; many infants asymptomatic at birth
GBSColonizes vagina/rectum; transmitted during childbirth; can cause neonatal meningitis, pneumonia, and sepsis
Source limit
The supplied handout expands Toxoplasma, rubella, CMV, and GBS in detail. It lists HSV and “Other” within TORCH but does not provide the same detailed HSV syndrome breakdown in this file, so this companion does not add one from outside knowledge.

Folate deficiency and radiation

Folic acid

Critical to neural-tube closure, especially days 18–33. Deficiency is implicated in neural tube defects.

Ionizing radiation

Causes chromosomal damage/cell death, especially in rapidly proliferating cells. Handout associations: microcephaly, intellectual disability, growth restriction, malignancy.

8. Neural tube defects

Closure rule: neural tube closure is especially folate-dependent between days 18–33 and should be completed by the end of week 4 in this handout.
Cropped lecture visual: progressive neural-tube closure, with cranial and caudal neuropores visible during the process.
Detection
The handout lists fetal ultrasound, amniocentesis, and maternal/amniotic α-fetoprotein testing as ways to detect open neural tube defects.

Caudal neural tube / vertebral arch defects

Cropped schematic: occulta versus meningocele versus myelomeningocele.
DefectWhat the source says is present
Spina bifida occultaVertebral arch does not fuse; defect is skin-covered; often a tuft of hair
MeningoceleCyst-like sac contains meninges (and CSF)
MyelomeningoceleSac contains meninges + spinal cord and/or nerve roots

Cranial neuropore defects

DefectMechanism / anatomy in source
EncephaloceleBrain + meninges protrude through openings in skull; associated with failure of cranial neuropore closure
AnencephalyAbsence of major portion of brain, skull, and scalp from failure of cranial neuropore closure; infant dies soon after birth

Folic-acid prevention numbers in the handout notes

SituationDose/timing stated in sourceEffect stated
No family history0.4 mg daily beginning 3 months before conception and through pregnancy40–50% decrease in NTD occurrence
Positive family history4.0 mg daily prior to and during pregnancy70% decrease in recurrence
